topic.title: AI made the documents longer
topic.claim: AI was meant to make work faster; in most offices it made documents three times longer and decisions no quicker.
topic.moment: A meeting summary with six headings and a 'key takeaways' box nobody scrolls to.

turn.believed: AI at work is making people more productive.
turn.actually: It mostly makes people look thorough, so everyone produces more pages for others to skim.

topic.because: Length still looks like effort to a busy boss. When writing costs nothing, the reader pays the cost instead.
topic.payoff: Before you send the AI version, ask if you'd have written half of it by hand. If not, delete that half.
topic.behaviour: People paste AI-written notes, decks and emails that are longer than needed; colleagues feed them back into AI to summarise.
topic.mechanism: Effort is judged by volume, and AI makes volume free.
topic.group: Desk workers using AI tools daily
topic.send_to: The colleague whose emails got four bullet points longer this year.
topic.why_now: Most offices now have AI tools switched on by default, and the side effects are visible in every inbox.

score.why: Matches his belief that AI at work is used to look busy; the six-heading summary nobody reads is instantly familiar.

cover.headline: At most desks, AI's real product is [looking thorough]
cover.sub: Every meeting now ends in six headings nobody scrolls to.

paragraphs: At most desks, AI's real product is looking thorough.
slides.why_swipe: Looking thorough to whom, and what happened to getting work done?

paragraphs: It's right after the Tuesday status call. Before you've refilled your water bottle, the AI summary is in your inbox, with two seniors cc'd.
Six headings, an action items table, and a 'Key Takeaways' box with a little lightbulb emoji. The call itself was mostly "you're on mute."
slides.why_swipe: So how does the office react to a summary like that?

paragraphs: Your manager hits reply-all within a minute: "Great summary, very thorough 👏" You read it twice. It's the nicest thing anyone's said to you this quarter.
So next week, you send one too. Yours has seven headings and a section called *Next Steps & Ownership*.
slides.why_swipe: Your summary got longer. Who actually reads it?

paragraphs: Across the floor, a teammate pastes your summary into their own AI and types "give me this in 3 lines."
What comes back: "Team discussed timelines. Alignment needed. Follow-up planned." Your seven headings were written for them. They never saw one.
slides.why_swipe: So why does the long version keep winning?

paragraphs: Here's the part nobody says in the meeting. A busy boss can't check what's inside a summary. They can see how long it is, and length still looks like effort.
When writing costs nothing, the reader pays instead, one scroll at a time. **So everyone gets rewarded for adding, never for cutting.**
I've sent the long version too, knowing exactly who it was for.
slides.why_swipe: So what does that reward do to next week's summary?

paragraphs: The senior who never scrolled down to the lightbulb sends a thumbs up anyway. That one emoji does more for your summaries than any training session.
Next Tuesday yours has eight headings. Your teammate's AI just has a little more to shrink.
slides.why_swipe: So how much of that summary did the meeting actually need?

paragraphs: Open the last summary you sent. Cover every line you'd never have bothered to type by hand.
What's left fits in one sentence: the decision is still pending.
**That was the whole meeting. The other six headings were for the 👏.**

end.save: Come back to this right before you paste your next meeting summary.
end.send: The colleague whose emails got four bullet points longer this year.

draft.caption: What's the longest AI-written mail you've received for something that needed one line?
draft.alt_text: Carousel post. Cover headline: At most desks, AI's real product is looking thorough. Sub-line: Every meeting now ends in six headings nobody scrolls to. The slides follow the reader after a Tuesday status call that was mostly people saying 'you're on mute'. An AI meeting summary arrives with six headings, an action items table and a key takeaways box with a lightbulb emoji, with seniors cc'd. The manager replies 'Great summary, very thorough' and the reader starts sending longer summaries too. A teammate pastes the summary into their own AI for three bland lines and never sees the headings. The writer explains that a busy boss judges length, not content, so everyone is rewarded for adding, and admits he has sent long versions too. A senior's thumbs up keeps the summaries growing each week. The last slide asks the reader to cover every line they'd never have typed by hand: what's left is one sentence saying the decision is still pending, and the rest was for the applause.
